Learning Objectives
Assess spinal embryology, anatomy, and physiology. 
Review applied surgical anatomy of the spine relevant to surgical exposures. 
Review traditional surgical approaches and newer techniques and develop an understanding
of safe placement of spinal instrumentation.


Overview

supporting soft tissue, and neurologic elements. To diagnose and treat patients with

spinal pathology, surgeons must have a strong understanding of spinal anatomy and
safely apply this knowledge to surgical approaches for and instrumentation of the spine.
Osteology
Spinal Development
All vertebrae have three primary ossification centers: the centrum (anterior vertebral body),
the neural arch (posterior elements, pedicles, and a small portion of the anterior vertebra),
and the costal element (anterior part of the lateral mass, transverse process, or rib).
In the intervertebral disk, the nucleus pulposus develops from the notochord, and the anulus
fibrosus develops from the sclerotome.

Spinal Development
The spinal column originates from pairs of mesodermal structures called somites.
Somites have three layers: the sclerotome, which becomes the vertebral bodies and the
anulus fibrosus; the myotome, which leads to myoblasts; and the dermatome, which
becomes skin. In the intervertebral disk, the nucleus pulposus develops from the
notochord, and the anulus fibrosus develops from the sclerotome. The C2 vertebral
body develops from five ossification centers, with an initial cartilaginous junction
between the dens and the vertebral body that fuses at age 7 years.
Cervical Vertebrae
The C1 (atlas) vertebra has no body or spinous process; instead, it has a posterior tubercle and
two lateral masses.
The C2 vertebra has the odontoid process (dens), which articulates with the anterior ring of C1.
The spinous processes are bifid (except C7 and sometimes C6).
C7 has a long, prominent spinous process (called the vertebra prominens).


Cervical Vertebrae
The occiput-C1 articulation is responsible for the greatest amount of neck flexion and
extension (50% of total). The atlantoaxial (C1-C2) joint is responsible for the greatest
amount of neck rotation (50% of total).
Thoracic Vertebrae
Angled spinous processes overlap substantially.
Costal facets (articulations of the ribs with the vertebral segments) are present on all vertebral
bodies and the transverse processes of T1 through T9.

Thoracic Vertebrae
The thoracic spine is unique because of articulation with the rib cage. This also makes
the thoracic spine the most rigid region of the axial skeleton. Costal facets (articulations
of the ribs with the vertebral segments) are present on all vertebral bodies and the
transverse processes of T1 through T9.
Lumbar Vertebrae
The lumbar vertebrae have large bodies with rectangular, nonoverlapping spinous processes.
Typically, L1 and L2 have smaller pedicles than T11 and T12.
The number of non–rib-bearing vertebrae varies, and preoperative knowledge of this
transitional anatomy is essential to perform surgery at the appropriate level.

Lumbar Vertebrae
The lumbar vertebrae have large bodies with rectangular, nonoverlapping spinous
processes. The number of non–rib-bearing vertebrae varies, and preoperative

knowledge of this transitional anatomy is essential to perform surgery at the appropriate
level. Sacralization of L5 occurs in approximately 2% to 15% of patients. Lumbarization of
S1 occurs in approximately 3% to 7% of patients. Bertolotti syndrome is characterized by
a large L5 transverse process that articulates with the sacrum. The prevalence of
Bertolotti syndrome is approximately 5%. Bertolotti syndrome may be a cause of back
pain in younger patients. A defect in the pars articularis is known as spondylolysis, which
may lead to spondylolisthesis. Spondylolysis is the most common cause of back pain in
young patients.
Sacrum
The sacrum is a single structure formed by the five fused embryologic sacral vertebrae. It has
four sacral foramina through which the S1 through S4 nerve roots run.
The broad superior sacral ala is similar to the transverse process of the more superior spine
and is a major target for lumbosacral fusion graft material.
Coccyx
The coccyx is formed by the fusion of the lowest four spinal elements.
Vasculature
Vertebral Artery
Branches from the subclavian
The vertebral artery enters the foramen transversarium of C6 in approximately 92% of
patients. Anomalous arteries may enter at C5 or C7, may be hypoplastic, or may be absent.
Vertebral artery anatomy at C1-2
The vertebral artery emerges from the transverse foramen of C2 and traverses laterally to
the transverse foramen of C1.
Exits the transverse foramen of C1 and makes a 90° turn (Figure 1)
Traverses within the groove on the superior surface of the posterior arch of C1 before
passing ventromedially around the spinal cord and through the foramen magnum before
uniting at the basilar artery
The distance from the C1 midline to the medial edge of the groove is 14 to 20 mm.

The ponticulus posticus is the bony arch that may form as a result of ossification of the
posterior occipital ligament, encasing the suboccipital nerve and the vertebral artery near
the vertebral artery groove.

IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 3-15.)

Dorsal branches supply the dura and posterior elements
Ventral branches supply the vertebral bodies
Artery of Adamkiewicz
The artery of Adamkiewicz is the dominant segmental artery in the thoracic spine. The artery
enters through the left intervertebral foramen from T8 to T12.
Supplies anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord

Artery of Adamkiewicz
In the spinal canal, the anterior spinal artery may be an amalgamation of segmental
arteries and collateral circulation rather than one contiguous structure, especially in
watershed regions, such as in the thoracic spine. The dominant segmental artery in the
thoracic spine often is called the artery of Adamkiewicz. This artery typically enters
through the left intervertebral foramen in the region of T8 to T12; however, anatomy
varies between individuals. This dominant artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the
spinal cord in this region. Disruption of the blood supply as a result of trauma or
iatrogenic injury may result in catastrophic compromise of spinal cord function.
Nerves
Spinal Cord
Early embryologic development (Resource 1; Figure 2)
During the third week of development, the embryo assumes a planar structure before the true
development of the central nervous system.
The primitive streak deepens to form the primitive groove. This midsagittal groove deepens
within the ectoderm and begins to fold onto itself, forming a neural tube.
As it closes, the neural crest forms dorsal to the neural tube, whereas the notochord remains
ventral to the neural tube.
The neural crest forms the peripheral nervous system (also the pia mater, spinal ganglia, and
sympathetic trunk).

The neural tube forms the spinal cord.
The notochord forms the anterior vertebral bodies and the intervertebral disks.
Structural anatomy
The spinal cord extends from the brainstem to L1.
Terminates at the conus medullaris
Surrounded by three layers of tissue termed the meninges, which consist of the pia mater,
arachnoid mater, and dura mater (Figure 3)
Functional anatomy (Figure 4)
The dorsal columns transfer vibration, deep touch sensation, and proprioception.
The lateral spinothalamic tract transmits pain and temperature sensation.
The ventral spinothalamic tract transmits light touch sensation.
Voluntary motor function is transmitted by the lateral corticospinal tracts, with the tracts for
the lower extremities, torso, and upper extremities running superficial to deep.
Sacral structures are the most peripheral in the lateral corticospinal tract; cervical structures
are more medial.


Spinal Cord
The spinal cord extends from the foramen magnum into the vertebral canal, which is a
bony corridor defined anteriorly by the posterior vertebral bodies and disks, laterally by
the pedicles and the lateral masses, and posteriorly by the lamina and the ligamentum
flavum. The vertebral canal is wider in the mediolateral direction than in the
anteroposterior direction at all levels in the cervical spine. The width is relatively
constant from C2 to C7 (approximately 23 to 26 mm).1 The spinal cord is widest at the C4
level (mean width, 13.3 mm), tapering off to 11.5 mm at C1 and 11 mm at C7.2
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Anatomy of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003024

The spinal cord is surrounded by three layers of connective tissue termed the
meninges.3, 4 The pia mater lies closest to the spinal cord and forms the denticulate
ligaments, which attach to the arachnoid and the dura mater, helping to stabilize it in
space. The second layer, the arachnoid mater, overlies the pia mater and is continuous
with the cerebral arachnoid. A fenestrated intermediate layer between the pia mater and
arachnoid mater forms a meshwork of ligaments attaching the spinal cord to the
arachnoid mater. Cerebrospinal fluid runs in the subarachnoid space. The dura mater is
the outermost layer surrounding the spinal cord.
Nerve Roots
In total, 31 paired spinal nerves are present: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1
coccygeal.
In the cervical spine, the numbered nerve exits at the level above the corresponding pedicle
(eg, the C4 nerve exits between C3 and C4).
In the lumber spine, the numbered nerve exits at the level below the corresponding pedicle
(eg, the L4 nerve exits between L4 and L5).

Nerve Roots
The nerve roots exit the spinal cord at the anterolateral sulcus (motor or ventral rootlets)
and the posterolateral sulcus (sensory or dorsal rootlets), uniting into the dorsal and
ventral nerve roots.5 The ventral and dorsal nerve roots are surrounded by their own pia
mater and run in a sleeve of dura and arachnoid mater, which then fuses with the
epineurium as it exits the neural foramen and forms a spinal nerve. The dorsal root
ganglion is a thickening in the dorsal root, usually in the neural foramen, that contains
numerous sensory (afferent) nerve cell bodies. The roots fuse shortly after, forming the
spinal nerve proper within the neural foramen, and then splits into dorsal and ventral
rami. The early sinuvertebral (recurrent meningeal) branches quickly innervate the facet
joints, anulus fibrosus, posterior longitudinal ligament (PLL), and periosteum of the
vertebral canal.5-7

Autonomic Nervous System
Sympathetic

Sympathetic
In total, 22 ganglia are present: 3 cervical, 11 thoracic, 4 lumbar, and 4 sacral.
In the cervical spine, the ganglia lie posterior to the carotid sheath on the longus capitis
muscle and the transverse processes. Stellate, middle, and superior ganglions are
present. The middle ganglion is the most surgically at risk at C6, the location at which it is
close to the medial border of the longus colli. Damage to the sympathetic nervous
system may result in Horner syndrome. Horner syndrome may occur after damage to
the inferior ganglia of the sympathetic chain lateral to the longus colli and consists of
ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis.
Parasympathetic

Parasympathetic
In the lumbar spine anterior to the lower lumbar vertebra, the parasympathetic fibers
from the S2, S3, and S4 levels form the pelvic splanchnic nerves and combine with the
sympathetic lumbar splanchnic nerves to form the hypogastric plexus. These structures
are at risk during anterior approaches to the lumbosacral junction and may result in
complications such as retrograde ejaculation if damaged.
Ligaments and Joints
Spinal Ligaments
Ligaments, which are present throughout the spine, contribute to the static stability of the
spine.
Anterior longitudinal ligament
The PLL is thicker over the vertebral body and thinner over the disks.
SEND FEEDBACK

Interspinous and supraspinous ligaments provide posterior ligamentous stability.
Ligamentum flavum
A particular arrangement of three ligaments forms the transverse cruciate apical alar ligament
complex at the C1-2 articulation

Spinal Ligaments
Ligaments, which are present throughout the spine, contribute to the static stability of
the spine (Figure 5). A particular arrangement of three ligaments forms the transverse
cruciate apical alar ligament complex at the C1-2 articulation (Figure 6). The transverse
ligament runs horizontally behind the dens and is the major stabilizer of the C1-C2 joint.
It is crossed (hence cruciate) anteriorly by the vertically oriented apical ligament. Finally,
a paired set of obliquely oriented alar ligaments adds support to the articulation.
The PLL is thicker over the body and thinner over the disks. Therefore, most disk
herniations occur lateral to the PLL at the disk level. The ligamentum flavum is a yellow,
elastic ligament connecting laminae but is not a contiguous structure. The ligamentum
flavum attaches cranially under the lamina at the level of the pars interarticularis and
caudally at the superior ridge of the lamina. Hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum is a
substantial contributing factor in degenerative spinal stenosis.
The facet joint capsule is thought to be innervated by the nerve to the facet capsule; the
anterior longitudinal ligament, PLL, and disk are innervated by the sinuvertebral nerve.
All of these are thought to contribute to discogenic/degenerative pain syndromes.

Facet (Apophyseal) Joints
The orientation of these joints varies throughout the spine based on the predominant
direction of allowed motion at that level. Although a smooth transition exists throughout the

spine, the degree of motion allowed in each spine region is approximately as follows:
Cervical: 0° coronal, 45° sagittal
Thoracic: 20° coronal, 55° sagittal
Lumbar: 50° coronal, 90° sagittal

Facet (Apophyseal) Joints
Also called the zygapophyseal joints, the facet joints are the articulating components of
the functional spinal unit. In the cervical spine, the superior articular facet is anterior and
inferior to the inferior articular process of the caudal level. In the lumbar spine, the
superior articular facet is anterior and lateral to the inferior articular process of the
caudal level.
Musculature
Anterior Neck
Superficially, platysma muscle (innervated by the seventh cranial nerve)
Stylohyoid and digastric muscles (innervated by the seventh cranial nerve)
Strap muscles, which include the sternohyoid and omohyoid in the superficial layer and the
thyrohyoid and sternohyoid in the deep layer (innervated by the ansa cervicalis)
Sternocleidomastoid (innervated by the eleventh cervical nerve and the ansa cervicalis) rotates
the head to the contralateral side and runs obliquely across the neck
Posterior Neck
Superficial layer: trapezius, levator scapulae
Intermediate layer: splenius capitis and erector spinae groups (spinalis, longissimus,
iliocostalis)
Deep layer: spinotransverse group (rotatores, multifidus, semispinalis)
Back
Superficial layer: trapezius superiorly, latissimus dorsi inferiorly

Intermediate layer: rhomboids and levator scapulae
Deep layer: erector spinae and transversospinalis (multifidus, longissimus, semispinalis)
Surgical Approaches
Anterior Cervical Approach
This approach involves the use of a plane between the strap muscles, trachea, and esophagus
medially and the sternocleidomastoid and the carotid sheath laterally.
The recurrent and superior laryngeal nerves are at risk of injury during this approach. Injury
may lead to temporary or permanent vocal cord paralysis.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) is a branch of the vagus nerve/tenth cranial nerve.
On the left, it turns beneath the aortic arch and ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove.
On the right, it crosses under the subclavian artery and enters the tracheoesophageal groove
higher in the cervical spine with a more variable course.
Injury to the superior laryngeal nerve may damage the mucosal sensory reflex, which
prevents aspiration.
Cutaneous landmarks for the anterior approach
The cricoid membrane at C5-6
The prominence of the thyroid cartilage at C4-5
The hyoid bone at C3
The angle of the mandible at C2

Anterior Cervical Approach
The anterior cervical approach is one of the most common approaches used during
spine surgery and is most frequently used for anterior cervical diskectomy and fusion.
After incising or dissecting through the platysma muscle, the deep cervical fascia (DCF) is
encountered. The DCF consists of three layers: superficial, pretracheal, and
prevertebral.8 Initially, the superficial and pretracheal DCF directly medial to the
sternocleidomastoid muscle are incised. At this stage superficially, the strap muscles
(covered with pretracheal DCF) are retracted medially, and the sternocleidomastoid
(covered with superficial DCF) is retracted laterally. This affords access to the poststyloid
visceral space, which lies between the carotid sheath laterally and the visceral fascia
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Anatomy of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003024
17/38

medially. The visceral fascia houses the thyroid gland, trachea, and esophagus. At this
stage when exposing the spine between C5 and C6, the omohyoid muscle traverses
laterally. It may be dissected and retracted or bisected if necessary for larger exposures.
During dissection through the visceral space, the recurrent and superior laryngeal
nerves are at risk of injury. The RLN is a branch of the vagus nerve (tenth cranial nerve).
The risk of RLN injury ranges from 2% to 14%.9 The left and right RLNs have different
courses. On the left, it turns beneath the aortic arch and ascends in the
tracheoesophageal groove. On the right, it crosses under the subclavian artery and
enters the tracheoesophageal groove higher in the cervical spine with a more variable
course. Historically, a left-sided approach has been proposed to result in a lower rate of
RLN injury because of its lower entry into the tracheoesophageal groove and its more
predictable course; however, this has not been confirmed in current studies.9
The next plane that is met is the prevertebral DCF, which overlies the vertebra and the
paired longus colli. Care must be taken to ensure that the prevertebral DCF is incised in
the midline, which can be achieved by ensuring that the prevertebral DCF is opened in a
region equidistant from both longus colli muscles. Subperiosteal dissection of the longus
colli muscles is then performed medial to lateral to expose the anterior vertebral bodies
and place the retractors. Care must be taken to ensure that exposure is not too lateral,
risking the vertebral artery. Initial exposure should not be more lateral than the medial
edge of the uncinate process; however, much anatomic variability exists.10 Lastly, care
must be taken to ensure no anomalous vertebral artery anatomy is observed on
preoperative imaging studies. Subperiosteal dissection of the longus colli muscles must
be performed from medial to lateral because the sympathetic trunk runs approximately
1 cm lateral to the medial insertion of the longus colli. Dissection along the course of the
sympathetic trunk may result in postoperative Horner syndrome. During dissection on
the left along the anterior vertebral bodies below C5, care must be taken to ensure no
thoracic duct injury occurs. The incidence of iatrogenic thoracic duct injury in one series
was 0.02%, with both patients undergoing left-sided C5-6 anterior cervical diskectomy
and fusion.11
Some cutaneous landmarks may help guide the approach to certain levels. Placement of
an incision at the level of the cricoid membrane usually is consistent with a C5-6 level.

9/3/26, 7:19 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003024

The prominence of the thyroid cartilage overlies C4-5. The hyoid bone is at the C3 level.
The angle of the mandible is at the C2 level. Regardless, variability between patients is
great enough to warrant radiographic assistance for localization.
Posterior Cervical Approach
A longitudinal incision is made through the skin and down to the ligamentum
nuchae/supraspinous ligament.
Following the bone of the spinous process, the surgeon can dissect down to the cervical
lamina and out onto the lateral masses as necessary.
Dissection anterolateral to the posterolateral margin of the lateral masses places the vertebral
artery at risk of injury, especially proximal to the C2 lateral mass.

Posterior Cervical Approach
The posterior cervical approach is used for many procedures, including cervical
laminectomies, fusions, and foraminotomies. A longitudinal incision is made through the
skin and the ligamentum nuchae/supraspinous ligament, with care taken to go through
the midline avascular raphe to minimize bleeding. The spinous processes of the cervical
vertebra are reached. Spinous processes of cervical vertebra are commonly bifid. Care
must be taken during dissection within the bifid spinous process because some patients
will have thin or no bone in that area.
Following the bone of the spinous process, the surgeon can dissect down to the cervical
lamina and out onto the lateral masses as necessary. The spinous process may be
minimal or nonexistent at C1; in this situation, the posterior arch of C1 is the starting
point for lateral dissection. In contrast to the subaxial spine, the interlaminar distance
between the occiput and C1 and C1-2 may be large enough that care must be taken to
always follow the bone of the vertebra during exposure to ensure no durotomy or spinal
cord violation. This is especially important between C1-2, the location at which the C2
nerve roots exit inferior to the C1 posterior arch and are at risk for injury during
dissection.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Anatomy of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003024
19/38

Exposure anterolateral to the posterolateral margin of the lateral masses places the
vertebral artery at risk of injury, especially proximal to the C2 lateral mass or in patients
with aberrant vascular anatomy. Similarly, dissection on the superolateral aspect of the
C1 posterior arch places the vertebral artery at risk. Preoperative imaging studies must
be assessed to rule out aberrant anatomy and to determine if one vertebral artery is
dominant or the vertebral arteries are codominant. This information is important in the
management of vertebral artery injuries that occur intraoperatively.
Anterolateral Thoracolumbar Approach
The rib that is two levels caudal to the vertebral body being approached (ie, T7 rib for T5
vertebral body) is selected. The skin is incised along with the posterior musculature, and
dissection is carried down to the rib itself.
With a transpleural approach, incision through the anterior periosteum and parietal pleura
affords access to the thoracic cavity.
Resection of the rib head affords visualization of the foramina and pedicle in addition to
demarcation of the depth of the posterior vertebral body.
The segmental arteries must be identified at the waist of the midbody between the
intervertebral disks. These may be ligated after identification.
More inferiorly, the diaphragm may be taken down by incising through its tendon 1 to 2 cm
from the lateral insertion.
More medial incision risks injury to the phrenic nerve and the muscle of the diaphragm.
The lumbar plexus runs through the posterior two-thirds and around the psoas muscle, with
the genitofemoral nerve directly anterior.
The lumbar plexus; the ureters; and, more distally, the iliac vessels are at risk of injury.

Anterolateral Thoracolumbar Approach
The anterolateral thoracolumbar approach is a mainstay approach for the management
of central anterior lesions that cannot be safely managed via a posterior approach. An
example of a lesion that likely requires management via the anterolateral thoracolumbar
approach is a central, large thoracic disk herniation. Anatomic considerations include the
laterality of the approach, which ultimately depends on specific patient anatomy.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Anatomy of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003024
20/38

Typically, a left-sided approach is used unless performed at T4-5 or higher, at which the
mediastinum may preclude safe approach.12 In these higher levels, a right-sided
approach or an anterior approach with a sternotomy may be necessary.12 Inferiorly, the
diaphragm is present at T12-L1; therefore, lesions about or below that level may require
releasing or cutting the diaphragm and a combined retroperitoneal approach. Incision
placement is guided by intraoperative localization via radiographic assistance; however,
an approximate estimate is that the rib that is two levels caudal to the vertebral body
being approached (ie, T7 rib for T5 vertebral body) is selected. The skin is incised along
with the posterior musculature, and dissection is carried down to the rib itself.
Subperiosteal dissection is performed about the rib anteriorly, with care taken to avoid
the neurovascular bundle on the inferior surface of each rib. The rib is then resected and
can be used for bone graft.
In a transpleural approach, incision through the anterior periosteum and the parietal
pleura affords access to the thoracic cavity. The rib heads articulate with the vertebral
body of the same level and the level above. At most levels, the rib head covers the disk
posterolaterally.12 The rib head overlies a portion of the foramen of the same level.12
For example, the fifth rib articulates with the transverse process of T5, the superior
aspect of the T5 body, and the inferior aspect of the T4 body.12 It overlies the T4-5
foramen and, therefore, the T5 nerve root.12 The sympathetic chain lies against the neck
of the ribs in the upper thorax but then moves ventrally along the lateral border of the
vertebra.12 The apex of the aortic arch is usually at T4, and the descending aorta is just
left of the midline. The thoracic duct is posterior and medial to the aorta.12 The azygous
vein is visualized with right-sided approaches and is right of the midline along the
anterior aspect of the vertebra.12 The azygous system is dissected anteriorly with the
vena cava via subpleural dissection on the lateral vertebral bodies. The hemiazygos vein
is a feeder vein into the azygous vein and is visualized with left-sided approaches. The
segmental arteries and veins must be identified at the body of the vertebra between the
intervertebral disks and may be ligated after identification. These vessels branch into
dorsal branches and more ventral intercostal arteries, which join the nerves at the
inferior aspect of the ribs.12 The dorsal branches give off a small radiculomedullary
branch that may constitute vascular anatomy to the spinal cord.12 The artery of
Adamkiewicz is a major radiculomedullary artery that has substantial blood supply to the
spinal cord. The artery of Adamkiewicz usually arises from the aorta from T8 to T10;

Lateral Lumbar Approaches
The lateral approach affords access to the anterior column of the spine from T12 to L5 without
requiring an access surgeon.
The transpsoas approach is through the psoas muscle, with care taken to traverse the psoas
muscle anterior to the lumbar plexus.
The pre-psoas approach is an oblique approach to the lumbar spine that is associated with
many of the advantages associated with the transpsoas approach but may result in fewer
complications because of the lack of psoas muscle and lumbar plexus irritation.

approach: external oblique, internal oblique, transverse abdominis into the retroperitoneal

The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves and the genitofemoral nerves are at risk as they
pass within the dissected layers or over the psoas, respectively.
Cadaver model studies have reported that approaches to the anterior two-thirds of the L4
vertebra and the anterior third of L5 are associated with the lowest risk of lumbar plexus nerve
injury.

Lateral Lumbar Approaches
The lateral approach to the lumbar spine affords access the anterior column of the spine
from T12-L5 without requiring an access surgeon. Lateral approaches to the lumbar
spine can be categorized as transpsoas and pre-psoas approaches. The transpsoas
approach is through the psoas muscle, with care taken to traverse the psoas muscle
anterior to the lumbar plexus. The pre-psoas approach is an oblique approach to the

lumbar spine that is associated with many of the same advantages associated with the
transpsoas approach but may result in fewer complications because of the lack of psoas
muscle and lumbar plexus irritation. The decision to proceed with one approach over the
other depends on surgeon comfort, the position of the iliac crest, the level of interest
and the position of the lumbar plexus within that level, psoas anatomy, and the amount
of space between the psoas muscle and the iliac vessels. This discussion is beyond the
scope of this topic because the focus is mainly on surgical anatomy.
These approaches begin with the same dissection, with the pre-psoas approach
associated with a more anterior incision because of the oblique nature of the approach.
The layers of fascia/muscle that are traversed to obtain access to the retroperitoneal
space are as follows: external oblique, internal oblique, and transverse abdominis. Care
must be taken during dissection through the fascial/muscle layers to ensure that no
injury to the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves occurs. After access to the
retroperitoneal space has been achieved, the peritoneum is retracted anteriorly, and the
psoas muscle is exposed. The genitofemoral nerve is observed running in a craniocaudal
direction on top of the psoas muscle until it continues anteriorly.
With the transpsoas approach, the spine must be accessed through a window free of any
nervous tissue. A cadaver model study reported that approaches to the anterior two-
thirds of the L4 vertebra and the anterior third of L5 are associated with the lowest risk
of lumbar plexus nerve injury.13 Another study reported that the safe corridors to
prevent injury to the femoral and genitofemoral nerves were the middle posterior
quarter at the L1-4 levels and at the midpoint of the L4-5 level.14 The transpsoas
approach is associated with an inherent risk of neurologic injury to the femoral nerve
and the lumbar plexus, with thigh dysesthesias, paresthesias, and numbness that may
occur with retraction. Iliopsoas dissection may result in hip flexor weakness. In most
patients, these symptoms are transient; however, the pre-psoas approach was created
to decrease some of the complications associated with traversing the psoas muscle.15 In
a pre-psoas approach, the peritoneum is mobilized more anteriorly. The ureter may be
visualized and will be attached to the posterior aspect of the peritoneum. Therefore, it is
mobilized anteriorly. The anterior aspect of the psoas muscle is then dissected off the
vertebral body, and the psoas muscle is mobilized posteriorly to expose the disk space.

Anterior Lumbar Approach
The anterior approach affords access to the anterior column of the lower lumbar spine. For
most spine surgeons, this approach requires an approach surgeon.
This approach is mostly used to access L5-S1.
Two anterior approaches to L5-S1 are used: transperitoneal and retroperitoneal.

Anterior Lumbar Approach
In general, the anterior approach to the lumbar spine is performed by an approach
surgeon who usually is a vascular or general surgeon. The anterior lumbar approach can
be performed via a transperitoneal or retroperitoneal approach. Most surgeons use a
retroperitoneal approach. The retroperitoneal approach begins by incising the anterior
fascia of the rectus abdominis muscle, usually via a left-sided approach. The rectus is
then retracted medially until the posterior fascia is identified. The transversalis fascia is
dissected to gain access to the retroperitoneal space. As the peritoneum is retracted
medially, the ureter is brought medially with it because it is attached to the posterior
aspect of the peritoneum. The psoas muscle is exposed. Medial to the psoas muscle is
the left iliac vessels. For L5-S1, the disk space is approached in the crotch of the vessels.
The middle sacral artery and vein are ligated and cut. The hypogastric plexus also is
present in this region. No cautery is used in ligating the middle sacral vessels to prevent
injury to the hypogastric plexus, which may result in retrograde ejaculation in males. For
L4-5 exposure, the iliolumbar vessels must be ligated to expose the disk space lateral to
the vessels. Failure to do this may result in catastrophic bleeding because the stump of
this iliolumbar vessel can retract into the psoas muscle. At L2-3 or L3-4, the approach is
lateral to the inferior vena cava and aorta.

Posterior Thoracic/Lumbar Approach
The posterior thoracic/lumbar approach is one of the most common approaches used in
spine surgery. The approach is used in laminectomies, laminotomies, foraminotomies,
and open fusions. Although intraoperative localization should always be confirmed
radiographically, the most common palpable landmark is the superior margin of the iliac
crest, which usually is at the L4-5 level. After the posterior thoracolumbar fascia is
reached, dissection is continued down the spinous processes in a subperiosteal plane to
remove the insertions of the paraspinal muscles off the spinous processes, lamina, facet
joints, and/or transverse processes. The transverse processes of the thoracolumbar
vertebrae are at the level of each facet joint, which is important to note during
placement of pedicle screws for arthrodesis.

Osseous Anatomy for Anterior Cervical Fixation
The safest approach to the anterior vertebral body is at the level of the superior end
plate/uncinate process because the anterior transverse process protects the vertebral artery.
No uncinate process is present at C7-T1.
Plates should be as short as possible for secure fixation to avoid injury to the adjacent disk
space. Placement of the plate at least 5 mm from the adjacent disk may minimize the risk of
adjacent-level ossification disease.

Osseous Anatomy for Anterior Cervical Fixation
The safest approach to the anterior vertebral body is at the level of the superior end
plate/uncinate process because the anterior transverse process protects the vertebral
artery. No uncinate process is present at C7-T1. From C2 to C6, the mean vertebral depth
is 15 to 17 mm, increasing distally. The sagittal diameter of the canal is 17 to 18 mm at
C3 to C6 and decreases to 15 mm at C7. Correspondingly, the distance between the
vertebral arteries decreases cephalad to caudad. In some patients, the course of the
vertebral artery may be medial, increasing the risk of vertebral artery injury during
cervical corpectomies. Preoperative evaluation of the course of the vertebral artery is
mandatory. Plates should be as short as possible for secure fixation to avoid injury to the
adjacent disk space. Placement of the plate at least 5 mm from the adjacent disk may
minimize the risk of adjacent-level ossification disease.

and C2 nerve roots at risk. The internal carotid artery lies anteriorly within 1 mm of the ideal
exit point of a bicortical C1 lateral mass screw or a C1-2 transarticular screw; however, few
complications have been reported.

Osseous Anatomy for Posterior Cervical Fixation
C1 lateral mass screw insertion places the vertebral and carotid arteries, hypoglossal
nerve, and C2 nerve roots at risk.16 The ideal starting point for a C1 lateral mass screw is
at the junction of the medial edge of the posterior arch attaching to the lateral mass,
with 10° to 15° of angulation upward and 5° to 10° of angulation medially.17,18 The
height for lateral mass screw placement, measured as the cephalad-caudad distance
from the bottom of the inferior facet to the top of the posterior arch at the vertebral
artery groove, is 8.99 mm, with a minimum height of 4.73 mm. In a study of 50 head and
neck CT scans, the mean distance from the internal carotid artery to C1 was
approximately 2.9 mm.19 The vertebral artery is at risk of injury with dissection of C1
laterally beyond 12 mm (cephalad). A ponticulus posticus is an anatomic variant
(prevalence, approximately 15%) characterized by an arcuate foramen at the arch of C1.
Injury to the vertebral artery may occur if this variant is not identified before
instrumentation of C1. The mean height of the C2 pedicle is approximately 8.7 mm, with
a mean width of 5.8 mm and an overall transverse angle of 43.2°, which makes it a
robust option for C2 pedicle screw placement.20,21 The safe site of screw entry is the
superior and medial third of the posterior surface of the C2 pedicle. The safe trajectory
for a C2 pedicle screw is 40° medial and 20° superior.22 Translaminar axis screws are a
robust option if fixation through the C2 pedicle or pars is problematic from an anatomic
or technical perspective.23-25 At C2, a unilateral anomalous vertebral artery is present in
18% of individuals, resulting in narrowing of the C2 pedicle and lateral mass. Careful
examination of preoperative CT scans is necessary to determine if C2 pedicle or
transarticular C1-2 fixation is feasible. With age, the course of the artery may encroach
on the C1-2 joint, making transarticular fixation impossible. The width of the inferior
surface of the isthmus is the most important measurement to obtain to avoid the

Osseous Anatomy for Lumbar and Sacral Fixation
The midpoint of the transverse process usually is at the superoinferior midpoint of the pedicle.
From L2 to L4, the medial border of the pedicle is in line with the lateral border of the pars.
Pedicle angulations increase from 12° at L1 to 30° at L5.

Osseous Anatomy for Lumbar and Sacral Fixation
Transpedicular screw fixation has become the standard technique for lumbar spine
instrumentation because it affords increased strength and stiffness with three-column
vertebral fixation. The lumbar pedicle screw entry point is at the midpoint of the
transverse process and the lateral border of the pars. From L2 to L4, the medial border
of the pedicle is in line with the lateral border of the pars. Pedicles angulate more medial
in the cephalad lumbar region. Pedicle angulations increase from 12° at L1 to 30° at L5.
In general, the L1 pedicle has the smallest diameter in the lumbar spine and is smaller
than the lower thoracic pedicles. The S1 pedicle is quite broad (19 mm) and has an
angulation of 39°. Bicortical transpedicular fixation is common at S1 to increase pullout
strength.

Pelvic fixation increases the rate of fusion across long constructs via fixation across the
center of rotation of the pelvis and out of the plane of the remainder of the construct.
Iliac bolts, although straightforward to place, often are not in line with the remainder of
the construct and require medial connectors. In addition, they may be prominent and
irritate the patient during certain activities and while in a seated position. The starting
point for iliac screws is just medial to the posterior superior iliac spine.
The iliac bolts consist of long, large-diameter screws inserted between the tables of the
ilium in a caudal (20° to 45°) and lateral (30° to 45°) trajectory. The use of S2-alar-iliac
screws overcomes these difficulties by allowing screw heads to be aligned with the
remainder of the construct, and S2-alar-iliac screws usually are deep enough to not be
symptomatically prominent. Both techniques are biomechanically equivalent.28 The
starting point for S2-alar-iliac fixation is 2 to 4 mm lateral and 4 to 8 mm caudal to the S1
foramen. The trajectory is toward the greater trochanter, with passage through the
sacral ala into the pelvis.
